Spiro Agnew was the thirty-ninth Vice President of the United States under Richard Nixon, serving from nineteen sixty-nine to nineteen seventy-three. He was a controversial figure who embodied Nixon's appeal to social conservatism and working-class resentment. Before becoming Vice President, Agnew served as Governor of Maryland from nineteen sixty-seven to nineteen sixty-nine and built a reputation as a tough-on-crime conservative, appealing to Nixon's "silent majority." Known for aggressive rhetorical attacks on the press, antiwar protesters, and intellectuals, Agnew coined phrases like "nattering nabobs of negativism" and "effete corps of impudent snobs." His vice presidency was marked by outspoken cultural criticism that resonated with conservative voters. However, Agnew's career ended abruptly. He resigned the vice presidency in October nineteen seventy-three after pleading no contest to tax evasion. He had accepted bribes throughout his political career as Maryland governor and county executive. His resignation occurred while Watergate was unfolding and preceded Nixon's own downfall. Agnew became a symbol of both Republican ruthlessness and the corruption of the Nixon era, his fall mirroring the president's own. After his resignation, he returned to private law practice and business, living quietly until his death in nineteen ninety-six, largely removed from public life. He remains the only Vice President to resign due to criminal charges.
